summary: This informational document considers what happens to video distribution if the underlying network moves from today's Internet to an Information-Centric Networking architecture. Since most future traffic is expected to be video, it looks at how existing adaptive streaming mechanisms would need to change. It discusses several approaches and open issues.

plainLanguage.summary: Watching a video online means asking a far-away computer for each piece. In a data-named network, any nearby copy can answer. This explores how video that adjusts its quality would work in such a network.

questions: how does video streaming work in icn
p2p video distribution in information-centric networks
subtitle: How video streaming protocols must adapt to work over Information-Centric Networks.

tldr.problem: Video will dominate future Internet traffic, but the current Internet architecture uses host-to-host connections that are inefficient for content distribution. Information-Centric Networking (ICN) retrieves content by name instead of location, but existing video streaming protocols like DASH were designed for the host-based Internet.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC explores how to adapt video streaming to work over ICN: running DASH over Content-Centric Networks, supporting P2P distribution through ICN's pull-based model, managing IPTV's strict latency requirements, and implementing digital rights management in a network where content is cached everywhere.
tldr.outcome: The document identifies key challenges and research directions for video streaming in ICN, including caching conflicts, bandwidth estimation changes, and synchronization issues.

today: RFC 7933 is an Informational RFC published in August 2016 by the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It remains the primary reference for video streaming considerations in ICN and continues to guide research on integrating multimedia delivery with information-centric architectures.

sections.title: Introduction and Use Cases
sections.content:
Video is expected to constitute the majority of Internet traffic in coming years. Today's Internet is built on host-to-host communication: to watch a video, your device connects to a specific server and asks for content. Information-Centric Networking (ICN) proposes a fundamentally different architecture where you request content by name, and the network returns it from wherever it is available—a nearby cache, another user, or the origin server.

This RFC examines what happens to video distribution when the network changes from host-centric to information-centric. It considers four main scenarios: on-demand video download (like Apple iTunes), adaptive video streaming (like Netflix), peer-to-peer video sharing, and IPTV broadcast. For each scenario, it identifies how existing protocols must change and what new challenges emerge in an ICN environment. The analysis focuses on practical issues like caching efficiency, bandwidth estimation, and synchronization that currently invisible in traditional networks but become critical in ICN.
sections.plainLanguage: When you watch Netflix, your phone calls a Netflix server. ICN would let you grab the video from any copy nearby. This document thinks through what that means.

sections.title: How DASH Would Work Over ICN
sections.content:
DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) is the dominant video streaming standard today. The client requests video segments of different quality levels based on available bandwidth and keeps its playback buffer at a safe level. DASH naturally aligns with ICN principles: it is pull-based (the client requests content), works with named segments, and already handles caching through Content Delivery Networks.

However, critical challenges arise. In traditional DASH, bandwidth estimation helps the client choose video quality; but in ICN, a chunk might come from a nearby cache, a distant server, or a different path entirely without the client knowing, making bandwidth estimates unreliable. DASH manifests list HTTP URLs; ICN would need names like ccnx:/netflix/episode1/segment42-1080p. Multiple video representations (different resolutions and bitrates) multiply caching burden: a cache must store all versions of each segment or lose efficiency. Additionally, ICN's implicit multicast and in-network caching can cause oscillations where clients rapidly switch between quality levels based on false signal about available bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: Netflix asks your network how fast you can download, then picks a video quality that fits. In ICN, you might grab the video from many places, making the network speed unclear. Netflix would get confused about quality and flip-flop.

sections.title: Peer-to-Peer Video Over ICN
sections.content:
P2P video distribution is naturally suited to ICN's pull-based model. The RFC discusses adapting PPSP (Peer-to-Peer Streaming Protocol) to work over ICN. In a P2P system, peers announce which video chunks they have available and request chunks from neighbors. ICN's content-by-name model aligns well with this: a peer requests ccnx:/swarmID/chunk/12 and the network returns it from whoever has it.

However, ICN poses a fundamental tension: peers need to know which other peers have which chunks (location-specific information), but ICN abstracts away location. The RFC describes two architectural approaches: a mediator approach where an adaptation layer translates traditional P2P messages to ICN, and a clean-slate approach where applications are rewritten to be ICN-native from the start. A critical challenge is the DASH representation problem: if many peers download different video quality levels independently, they cannot share chunks with each other, reducing collaboration efficiency. Using Scalable Video Coding (SVC), where quality layers progressively build on each other, allows peers at different quality levels to share base layers and improve collaboration.
sections.plainLanguage: In P2P, people call each other saying "I have chunk 5, do you have chunk 6?" ICN makes this work by name, but if everyone chooses a different quality level, they can't help each other. Using layered video (base + enhancements) lets them share the base.

sections.title: IPTV and Digital Rights Management
sections.content:
IPTV (Internet Protocol Television) adds stringent timing constraints beyond on-demand streaming. Channels must stream continuously with latency under 500 milliseconds, and packet loss must be extraordinarily low (less than 10^-7). ICN offers inherent benefits: implicit multicast, fast recovery from packet loss using in-network caches, and peers that can act as backup sources.

However, challenges emerge. ICN is pull-based (each client requests data), creating upstream messaging overhead. With IPTV streams at 15 Mbps or higher, even thousands of simultaneous viewers require a corresponding flood of requests upstream. Caching becomes problematic when content expires in one second; the system must intelligently flush old content without degrading other cached data. For Digital Rights Management (DRM), ICN's inherent caching creates a unique challenge: encrypted content can be cached by anyone, but the publisher needs to ensure only paying customers can decrypt it. The RFC discusses two approaches: Broadcast Encryption (where a single key serves multiple authorized users but revocation is expensive) and AAA-based DRM (where tokens issued to users link to network and caching provider policies, allowing shared decryption keys while maintaining access control).
sections.plainLanguage: Live TV needs to be super fast and super reliable. ICN helps by caching nearby and having neighbors help. But everyone keeps asking for the same channel (lots of upstream traffic), and you need to stop people from watching after they stop paying.

sections.title: Open Research Questions
sections.content:
The RFC concludes by identifying areas requiring further research. Large-scale live events (sports in stadiums, concerts) require content discovery in addition to delivery as users generate content on the fly and share it locally. Video conferencing and real-time communications over ICN introduce even stricter timing requirements and multi-source, multi-destination complexity. Store-and-forward optimized rate adaptation asks whether adaptation algorithms should be aware of in-network caches rather than just bandwidth.

Other open problems include heterogeneous wireless environments (where users have multiple network interfaces and can seamlessly switch between them), network coding (using mathematics to reduce redundant transmissions), and synchronization (ensuring multiple video layers and audio tracks stay in sync when they arrive from different sources). The document emphasizes that success requires not just adapting existing protocols but designing ICN-specific mechanisms that exploit the architecture's unique properties of location-agnostic content naming and ubiquitous caching.
sections.plainLanguage: Video calls, live events, smart networks that know about caches, and math tricks to send less data—these all need new research before ICN video will work perfectly.
